messages.subject: Instats launches AI Research Assistant – free, private and secure
messages.subject_clean: Instats launches AI Research Assistant – free, private and secure
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone

We've just launched a major upgrade to the Instats AI Research Assistant, giving researchers free, 24/7 access to leading AI technology to help with research methods, coding, writing, and much more in any language.

The Assistant is built directly into our research seminars, so you can engage leading experts and not only ask questions but also get support with your own research. Whether it's understanding difficult concepts, generating or debugging code, interpreting analyses, or applications to your own research the new AI research assistant is here to help!

It's designed with researchers' privacy, security, and intellectual property in mind – your chats live locally on your browser and are never used for AI model training.

Use it for free: We've made many our seminars including A Bit of AI – Best Tools for Research <https://instats.org/seminar/a-bit-of-ai-best-tools-for-research-free-1?viewassistant=yes> and the AI Research Assistant available free of charge. Register for the seminar and start asking questions directly alongside the video.

The Assistant is also included at no cost when taking any of our Instats certification programs <https://instats.org/results?view=Seminars&nav=Certifications>. Instats members enjoy unlimited access to the Assistant and more than 500 expert-led research training programs.

As an organization founded and led by academics, our goal is to make world-class research training and AI assistance accessible to researchers everywhere.

We hope you find it useful, and please feel free to share it with colleagues and students!

Best wishes

Michael Zyphur
Director and Co-founder
Instats | instats.org <http://instats.org>

messages.subject: Re: Reliability of a Second-Order Factor and Its Subdimensions – Which Values Should I Report?
messages.subject_clean: Reliability of a Second-Order Factor and Its Subdimensions – Which Values Should I Report?
messages.body_plain:
Following up on this thread to confirm that compRelSEM() no longer provides the reliability estimate for second-order factors, along with reliability estimates for the first-order factors, by including the higher = argument. Rather, to get a reliability estimate for the second-order factor, you need to use the W = argument with the custom weight syntax (https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/semTools/versions/0.5-9/topics/compRelSEM). Also, when the compRelSEM() function is used on a second-order CFA, are the values returned for each first-order factor interpreted as the omega reliability estimates for that first-order factor accounting for the second-order factor?

On Tuesday, April 1, 2025 at 2:57:06 PM UTC-4 lavaanrookie99 wrote:
>
> Dear Terrence,
>
> Thank you very much for your clarification! Indeed, the values match when I set obs.var = FALSE.
>
> I read the paper by Flora (2020) a few months ago and recall that it includes the option of calculating model-implied total variance. However, I must admit that I had forgotten about this option.
>
> Best regards,
> lavannrookie99
> Terrence Jorgensen schrieb am Dienstag, 1. April 2025 um 10:42:44 UTC+2:
> > > compRelSEM(fit_secondorder, higher = "Wellbeing", tau.eq = FALSE)
> > >
> > > Wellbeing: 0.787
> > >
> > >
> > > reliabilityL2(fit_secondorder, "Wellbeing")
> > >
> > > omegaL1: 0.7946842
> > > omegaL2: 0.9017477
> > > partialOmegaL1: 0.9037898
> > >
> > > My Questions:
> > >
> > > The reliability values differ depending on the function used.
> > The reason they differ is because the deprecated reliabilityL2() only calculated model-implied (rather than observed) total variance for the denominator, whereas the more general function gives you the choice.  The highlighted values above would match if you set compRelSEM(fit_secondorder, higher = "Wellbeing", obs.var = FALSE), which tells it to use model-implied total variance in the denominator.
> > >
> > > Also, the subscale reliabilities are different from when I compute them separately with ci.reliability. Which values should I report?
> > You didn't provide your ci.reliability() output, but that is only in the MBESS package now (it hasn't been part of semTools for several years).  But the point estimates are still provided by the deprecated reliability() function, which confusingly outputs several options that compRelSEM() makes possible but only if explicitly requested.  The reliability() output's "omega2" (also "omega" if the model has simple structure and no residual covariances) is what compRelSEM(obs.var=FALSE) provides, reliability() output's "omega3"  output is what compRelSEM() provides by default.  Also, unlike the deprecated functions, compRelSEM() provides both the higher-order and subscale reliabilities in the same output:
> >
> > Engagement_LV: 0.683
> > Perseverance_LV: 0.766
> > Optimism_LV: 0.714
> > Connectedness_LV: 0.748
> > Happiness_LV: 0.893
> > Wellbeing: 0.787
> >
> >
> > >
> > > Can I compute omega for the global Wellbeing sum score (the average of the subdimensions)?
> > That is what the highlighted values above represent: reliability of the sum or average of all observed indicators (i.e., the proportion of that composite's variance that is attributable to the higher-order factor).
> >
> > > Terrence D. Jorgensen    (he, him, his)
> > > Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> > > Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> > > http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
> >
